categories.name: From the rooms
categories.description: Notes from the people who set the tables.

posts.title: How we set a name card
posts.excerpt: Lucía Navarro sets every name card herself, and she starts at the head of the table.
posts.content:
Every name card in the house is set by Lucía Navarro, our floor manager. She starts at the head of the table with the host's card and works down both sides, checking each one against the plan the host has sent us, so that nobody ends up beside a stranger by accident.

The cards are blank until the host's list arrives, and they are written by hand in the afternoon briefing. On the night of a company dinner or a wedding party, the name cards and the tables are set by 17:30, half an hour before the first guest comes through the door at Harbour Steps.

If you would like the cards in a particular order, tell Aiyana when you ask about a date. A seating plan sent ten days ahead, with the final numbers, is all we need.

posts.title: A winter menu for forty
posts.excerpt: Teodor Brandt on cooking six courses for forty people at one table.
posts.content:
Cooking for forty at one table is a question of rhythm. Teodor Brandt, our head chef, plans a six-course company dinner so that no course waits more than a few minutes at the pass, and every plate leaves the kitchen at the same moment.

November's first course is a chestnut broth, poured at the table from a warm jug into dark stoneware bowls. It is followed by a cold fish course, a roasted root vegetable course, a shared main carved at the table, a cheese course and a pear dessert.

The company dinner menu is €84 per head, with printed menus and name cards included. Paired drinks, chosen by Samir Haddad, are €42 per head.

posts.title: Planning a toast that people hear
posts.excerpt: Kwame Mensah, maître d' for wedding parties, on where to stand and when to stop.
posts.content:
Kwame Mensah has run the Long Room for wedding parties for years, and his advice on toasts is short. Stand, wait for the room to settle, and speak to the far end of the table rather than the nearest guest.

In a wedding party of fifty, the toast comes first, standing, with a glass in every hand. Our floor team fills glasses quietly in the five minutes before, so that nobody leaves the room during the speech.

Speeches and a screen are welcome in the Long Room. Tell us what you plan when you ask about a date, and we will set the room with the right sightlines.
